title: Writing custom down
bodyMd:
When the communes of northern Italy began, in the twelfth century, to write their customs down, contemporaries described the act as a work of preservation. The statutes, they said, merely recorded what everyone already knew. Modern historians are more sceptical. Writing a custom down does not photograph it; it selects, abridges and freezes it, and in doing so it changes what the custom is.

Consider the difference in how a doubtful case is settled. An unwritten custom lives in the memory of elders and is applied by men who have watched it applied before. Its content is renegotiated, quietly, every time it is invoked: a hard case is decided, and the decision becomes part of the custom without anyone announcing an amendment. A written statute cannot work this way. Its words are fixed, and a hard case must therefore be resolved by interpreting those words rather than by consulting a shared recollection. The interpreter — increasingly, in this period, a trained jurist rather than a respected neighbour — acquires an authority that the oral system never conferred on any single person.

The communes' own drafters seem to have half-understood this. Many early statute books contain a clause instructing that where the written text is silent, the ancient custom is to be followed; some add that where the text is obscure, custom is to govern its reading. Such clauses are usually read as evidence of continuity. They may equally be read as evidence of anxiety: a drafter who feels the need to subordinate his text to something older is a drafter who suspects the text will not behave as he intends. Within two generations the clauses had largely disappeared, and where they survived they were themselves interpreted by jurists — which is to say, the older authority had been absorbed by the newer one.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage of about 330 words on the history of law. It argues that when twelfth-century northern Italian communes wrote their customary law into statutes, the act changed the custom rather than simply preserving it: fixed wording forced hard cases to be settled by interpreting text instead of by consulting shared memory, which gave trained jurists an authority no individual had held under the oral system. The final paragraph discusses clauses in early statute books directing that ancient custom govern where the text is silent or obscure, and offers two readings of them, continuity and anxiety, before noting that the clauses largely disappeared within two generations.

provenance.notes: Original prose written for this question bank. The historical setting is general background knowledge about medieval Italian communal statutes; no published passage, translation or scholarly text was copied, paraphrased or reconstructed.
